item.title: The context problem: How Docusign built agents that understand the business behind contracts
item.description:
Ask a general-purpose language model to summarize a contract, and it will probably do a reasonable job. Ask it to calculate what a company owes a supplier, accounting for three amendments, a revised pricing schedule, and an internal procurement policy, and it’s a different story.

Enterprise AI agents need to know more than what’s written in a document. They need context about which contracts belong together, which terms still apply, and when a decision needs human approval.

It’s a problem Docusign is tackling as it expands beyond electronic signatures into an Intelligent Agreement Management (IAM) platform.. Introduced in April 2024 and available in the U.S. to customers that May, the IAM platform helps organizations create, commit to and manage agreements.

At the center of that effort is Docusign Iris , the contract AI engine that powers Docusign IAM and its AI features across the agreement lifecycle. It combines Docusign’s contract management expertise, agreement-centric data, and AI models to help teams surface insights and take action across contract workflows.

“General LLMs are great. It’s just that you need more around it to really unleash its full power,” Sagnik Nandy , Docusign’s chief technology officer, tells The New Stack .

Docusign for Developers is a powerful suite of tools and resources designed to help developers build the solutions, workflows, and integrations their organizations and customers need across the entire agreement lifecycle.
Learn More

“Context is one of the things that really differentiates a generic solution from a solution that speaks your language.”

“Context is one of the things that really differentiates a generic solution from a solution that speaks your language.”

Four kinds of context

Nandy breaks context into four categories: within-agreement, cross-agreement, organizational, and user.

In Nandy’s account, the first is relatively straightforward: following a term defined on page two and referenced again on page 20 of the same contract. When that term appears across several contracts and amendments, working out which version applies becomes harder.

“…To an LLM, they look like three or four independent PDF files.”

“Imagine you have a single agreement that’s gone through two or three amendments, or a price change. To an LLM, they look like three or four independent PDF files,” Nandy explains.

In practice, those documents form a single contractual relationship. If someone asks about pricing, the system needs to identify the terms currently in force, not simply retrieve every price mentioned.

“You really have to bring them together. You need custom logic to even group them the right way,” he says.

That requires recognizing relationships between documents and understanding how amendments change the original terms. Retrieval alone isn’t enough to establish which version of a clause applies.

An AI contract agent also needs to understand the company’s internal policies. Legal might have a playbook spelling out which terms it will accept, while procurement and sales have different rules about who can approve what. Without that information, the agent wouldn’t know whether a contract meets the company’s requirements or needs sign-off.

The fourth category is user context, including someone’s language preferences, previous questions, and feedback.

According to Nandy, general-purpose LLMs may handle much of the first category, but the other three are considerably harder.

Building agreement intelligence

Iris combines several AI contracting capabilities rather than relying on a language model to do everything.

“Iris has a lot of pieces to it. It has everything from intelligent extractions. It has semantic search. It has a rich agentic layer. It has the ability to build agents. It has rich context,” Nandy says.

Finding a renewal date is one thing. Knowing whether the contract needs attention, based on its history and the company’s rules, is another.

Iris uses extraction to identify contract information, semantic search to find relevant agreements, and agreement-specific logic to connect contracts, amendments, and parties. Agents can then use that information to carry out tasks.

Consider a procurement manager asking which software contracts worth more than $1 million are due for renewal in the next three months.

Nandy says answering that question often previously involved multiple people gathering information, consolidating spreadsheets, and reconciling supplier names that appeared differently across agreements.

Iris can help find those contracts, identify upcoming obligations, and check agreements against organizational playbooks. It can also flag issues that might need attention before renewal.

Even a question about payment obligations to a particular supplier involves several steps. Iris needs to recognize the supplier as a company, find its agreements, account for amendments, and establish how the obligations have changed.

“While it seems like a straightforward question, to make it truly happen, you need rich search functionality. You need a repository,” Nandy says.

“You need this context of how these agreements are combined to create single entities, and then you need to make the search give the answer and the ability to iterate.”

“The beauty is to hide the complexity and make it look easy to the end user. But there’s a lot going on behind it.”

He estimates that answering such a question could involve five or six tools, drawing on Docusign’s contract-specific data and bringing the results together. “The beauty is to hide the complexity and make it look easy to the end user. But there’s a lot going on behind it.”

Knowing when to involve a human

Giving agents more context raises another question: how much should they be allowed to do?

Docusign combines agentic capabilities with business rules and approval processes, letting organizations decide which parts of a contract workflow to automate and where people remain in control.

For smaller renewals below a company’s spending threshold, an Iris-powered agent could gather and assess the agreement information, while a configured workflow applies the routing and approval rules. Higher-value contracts, or those with exceptions, could go to a person for review.

Nandy describes how “renewals below a certain threshold” might follow standard procedures, while more expensive or sensitive agreements would bring a person into the process.

Getting that wrong could mean approving terms that should have gone to legal, or overlooking obligations buried in an earlier agreement.

Docusign’s ready-to-deploy agents can be invoked through the Iris AI assistant in a chat experience or used as steps in Workflow Builder to retrieve agreement information, apply playbooks and monitor obligations.

Teams can also create custom AI contract agents in Docusign Agent Studio. Workflow Builder combines agent reasoning with rule-based routing and approvals ; the agent returns a result, and the workflow uses it to determine the next step. Availability varies by plan, region and language; Docusign currently lists the assistant and Agent Studio agents as part of eligible IAM plans in North America data centers, in English.

From documents to business decisions

Electronic signatures address one part of the contract process, but much of the work happens before and after signing.

Nandy splits the agreement lifecycle into three stages: creating an agreement, committing to it and managing it afterward.

For a new contract, that could mean knowing which templates to use and which terms the company typically agrees to. If negotiations lead to changes, the agent needs to check previous agreements and work out who has to approve them. Once the contract is signed, it should help teams track what they’ve agreed to and when the deal comes up for renewal.

Some Docusign customers are reporting improvements from bringing agreement information into their business processes, although those results aren’t necessarily attributable to autonomous agents.

In its 2026 Customer Awards , Docusign reports that Experian cut contract cycle times from roughly 10 days to hours and made contract data easier to access and understand by connecting Docusign with its configure-price-quote (CPQ) solution.

For developers building enterprise contract AI agents, Nandy’s examples show why the language model is only part of the job. The system also needs reliable contract data, a way to connect related documents, an understanding of company rules, and clear limits on what it can do without approval.

Reading a contract is relatively easy. Knowing what it means for the business is where the real engineering work begins.

item.title: Five years after the fork, OpenSearch is slowly stepping out of AWS’s shadow
item.description:
OpenSearch has come a long way since Amazon Web Services first announced the project back in January 2021, in response to Elastic’s decision to move Elasticsearch and its accompanying visualization tool, Kibana , away from Apache 2.0 and onto a combination of proprietary and source-available licenses. Elastic said at the time that the reason was to prevent cloud behemoths such as AWS from offering Elasticsearch “as a service” without giving anything back, while also accusing AWS of violating the Elasticsearch trademark .

While Elastic subsequently returned Elasticsearch and Kibana to open source by adding AGPL as a licensing option, making up with AWS along the way , OpenSearch has continued forging its own path as an independent open source project — albeit one still closely associated with the technology giant that created it.

Reducing the AWS dependency

A major milestone came in September 2024, when AWS transferred OpenSearch to the Linux Foundation , establishing the OpenSearch Software Foundation and placing the project under “vendor-neutral” governance. The move was intended to give other companies greater confidence that they could contribute to OpenSearch without AWS retaining ultimate control over its future.

Two years on, OpenSearch shows signs of gaining traction beyond its original backer. Figures provided to The New Stack by the OpenSearch Software Foundation show that AWS’s share of contribution activities across the project’s repositories has fallen from 91% in its first year to 72% in 2025–26. Meanwhile, Amazon-affiliated engineers accounted for 95% of maintainers in the core OpenSearch repository in April 2022 , compared with 71% today.

The shift is also visible in how organizations are deploying the software. In the 2026 Open Data Infrastructure Report , published last month by the Linux Foundation and the OpenSearch Software Foundation, data suggest that self-managed deployments have grown faster than Amazon’s managed OpenSearch Service since 2024. Some 60% of surveyed OpenSearch users now run self-managed deployments in the cloud, up from 37% in 2024, while use of Amazon’s managed service rose more modestly, from 44% to 48%.

Yet AWS’s historical association with OpenSearch remains an obstacle for some prospective users. According to the report, nearly a quarter (24%) of 71 surveyed non-adopters cite concerns about the project’s vendor neutrality and historical ties to AWS as reasons for staying away.

The figures point to a challenge that a change in governance alone cannot resolve: convincing prospective users and contributors that OpenSearch’s future is no longer determined primarily by AWS.

‘A watershed moment’ for OpenSearch

The New Stack caught up with Bianca Lewis , executive director of the OpenSearch Software Foundation, at Open Source Summit Europe in Prague this month to discuss the project’s evolution beyond its Elasticsearch origins, including any lingering perception of AWS influence.

Lewis argues that the project’s legal independence, achieved more than two years ago, provides an important foundation for building that trust.

“When they donated it to the Linux Foundation, that was a watershed moment.”

“When they donated it to the Linux Foundation, that was a watershed moment,” Lewis tells The New Stack . “Because they couldn’t close OpenSearch and they couldn’t change the license. They didn’t own the application anymore.”

Lewis also suggests the decision made commercial sense for AWS, whose cloud business generates revenue from the computing resources used to run applications, rather than necessarily owning the applications themselves.

“AWS don’t make money from applications,” she says. “AWS make money from compute. So operating, growing OpenSearch long term was never in AWS’s plan.”

“AWS don’t make money from applications. AWS make money from compute. So operating, growing OpenSearch long term was never in AWS’s plan.”

But questions remain about how much influence AWS continues to wield. The company still accounts for nearly three-quarters of recorded contribution activities across OpenSearch’s repositories. And while AWS holds just four of the 15 voting seats on the project’s Technical Steering Committee (TSC), an AWS employee, Andrew Ross , was just reelected committee chair in October.

The AI opportunity for OpenSearch

While AWS’s influence remains evident in OpenSearch’s governance, the software itself has changed considerably since the fork. And Lewis readily acknowledges just how closely it resembled Elasticsearch in the early days.

“It’s undeniable that the early versions of OpenSearch was Elasticsearch with a different name,” she says. “They had the same plugins. Even a lot of the documentation of OpenSearch was Elasticsearch documentation. [But] when it got donated to the Linux Foundation a couple years back, it had already well and truly diverged from its original mother project.”

Today, OpenSearch is positioning itself as infrastructure for applications that need to search, analyze and retrieve data, including those built around large language models (LLMs). Its support for vector and hybrid search, for example, makes it relevant to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where AI applications retrieve information from external sources to supplement model responses.

The project’s latest release, OpenSearch 3.9, which debuted in September , builds on those capabilities with improvements aimed at helping developers search and retrieve information for AI applications, alongside updates to performance, monitoring, and alerting.

Lewis believes this creates an opportunity for OpenSearch to become a central component of enterprise AI infrastructure.

“If you decide that you wanted your AI infrastructure on an open platform, I think [OpenSearch] today is just the default choice,” she says.

Winning the enterprise

Ambitions are one thing. Turning those ambitions into long-term enterprise adoption is something else entirely. The Foundation’s report indicates that a substantial proportion of OpenSearch deployments remain experimental, with organizations still evaluating the technology or using it for applications that could be replaced.

Asked about this, Lewis points to the amount of time it can take for companies to move away from established commercial platforms, particularly when they are tied to multiyear licensing agreements.

“They might have a three-year contract for Splunk, a license for five years with Elastic,” she says. “So they’re not just chucking that out.”

In other words, companies may be testing OpenSearch while continuing to use products they have already paid for. But there is, of course, no guarantee those evaluations will result in permanent deployments.

Lewis argues that one reason organizations might eventually make the switch is the freedom to change technology providers without having to rebuild their applications.

“What if I get locked in? And if I get locked in and I want to leave, what does that look like? Do I have to rearchitect all my applications?”

“What if I get locked in? And if I get locked in and I want to leave, what does that look like? Do I have to rearchitect all my applications?,” she says.

That concern extends beyond licensing costs. Enterprises must also consider the engineering effort involved in changing suppliers, moving data, and maintaining applications over time.

And this all brings the discussion back to the question of OpenSearch’s independence. If organizations are choosing the platform partly to avoid dependence on individual vendors, the project’s ability to attract and retain contributors beyond AWS becomes all the more important.

Asked what she hopes OpenSearch will look like five years from now, Lewis returns to the question of vendor influence — and her ambition for a project that no single company dominates.

“To have a truly sustainable, fast, innovating platform, which is not dominated or heavily influenced by any single vendor in the world,” she says. “Then, you’ve got a stable platform.”

item.title: Developers ask AI which tool to use. Here’s how we track the answer.
item.description:
We asked Claude “Which CMS platforms support MCP integration ?” It searched the web and put Webflow in its first group, Headless and SaaS CMS platforms with hosted MCP servers, sixth in the list, with this line: “A hosted server for managing sites through the Data API, covering pages, components, CMS collections and items, assets, forms, and publishing.”

Which CMS platforms support MCP integration?

We asked Claude the same question four times. That one was the most detailed of the four, so don’t read it as typical. Webflow got its own bullet in three of the four. Two of those answers said the server works with CMS collections and items, and one said only that it covers the Data API and the Designer. In the fourth run we were one name in a shared bullet with no description. Below, we count how often the engines name Webflow.

We asked because AI agents are already one of the ways developers look things up: in Stack Overflow’s 2026 developer survey , nearly 70% of respondents said they use an AI agent to help them find answers. We wanted to see what those agents say when the question is which tool to use.

AI picks a first answer for a lot of questions

Ask Claude what to use for transactional email and Resend comes up first. Ask what to use for product analytics and PostHog comes up first. We don’t have data on how many developers stop at the first name, but we’d rather be in that first answer than not.

Webflow is the agentic web marketing platform where AI and teams design, build, optimize, and publish in one governed system. Visual authoring, structured CMS, managed hosting, and developer extensibility through APIs, code components, and cloud deployments. Not just content. The full experience.
Learn More
The latest from Webflow
Designing APIs for agents Webflow MCP 2.0 is a big upgrade. Here's what it can do. Webflow Cloud. One workspace for your site and your app. Or just the app.
Hear more from our sponsor
What should I use for transactional email?

What should I use for product analytics?

CMS is the category we care about, and “I need to add a CMS to my website” is how we expect the question to sound. We ran it three times. Webflow was recommended once, last in its group. In the other two it was an example of what you might already use, or it wasn’t named. Sanity, Payload, WordPress, and Ghost showed up in all three. Our question is what it takes to be the default in that category, and we start by measuring where we are today.

I need to add a CMS to my website.

Why we track it

We follow one prompt closely, “Which CMS platforms support MCP integration?” Between Sep 25 and Oct 19 it ran 100 times, 25 on each of four engines. Webflow shows up in 49 of those 100 responses, but the spread by engine is wide, from 22 of 25 on Perplexity to 4 of 25 on Claude.

“When an engine leaves us out, the developer asking never sees Webflow, and nothing in our site analytics records it because the question was answered before anyone visited a page.”

When an engine leaves us out, the developer asking never sees Webflow, and nothing in our site analytics records it because the question was answered before anyone visited a page. We don’t have referral data that connects these answers to signups or revenue, so we aren’t claiming a revenue effect. What we can measure is whether we’re named, how we’re described, and which sources the engine used.

How we track it

We use Webflow AEO , under Insights > AEO. The Prompts page lists each tracked prompt with its topic, visibility score, citation rate, and the change from last week. Opening a prompt shows how many responses were tracked, citations split between owned and non-owned domains, citation rate by platform, which of our pages were cited, and a response log you can export.

Mention rate is how often Webflow shows up across the prompts we track. It counts a mention whether the description is right or wrong, so we also score the responses we review on four things: whether Webflow is named, which tier it’s placed in (official, community, or not listed), whether the description is accurate, and what type of source the engine used. The dashboard’s visibility score reads 47% for the last 30 days. Our 49 of 100 is a count of responses that named Webflow, so the two won’t match exactly.

We’re moving from single prompts to clusters of phrasings. Developers don’t type the same sentence, so we group several phrasings of one intent into a cluster and run each one on every engine repeatedly, then report rates and ranges for the cluster.

Each response becomes one row in our log. Here’s what one row looks like:

JSON
{
"date": "2026-10-21",
"engine": "Claude",
"prompt": "Which CMS platforms support MCP integration?",
"mentioned": true,
"position": 6,
"listed_total": 18,
"section": "Site builders and hosted platforms",
"tier": null,
"accurate": null,
"cited_sources": [
"sanity.io",
"developersdigest.tech",
"strapi.io",
"crox.io",
"themeisle.com",
"magazine.joomla.org"
]
}

We leave accurate empty until someone checks the description against our docs, which keeps a confident-sounding answer from being counted as a correct one. tier is empty here because the answer never labeled Webflow official or community.

What the four engines said

These are the responses AEO tracked on the same morning, quoted exactly.

Claude gave Webflow one line under “Website Builders / E-commerce CMS,” “Has an official remote MCP server with OAuth support,” and named it in the closing summary of platforms “generally cited as having the most mature official implementations.” The answer is short, and none of the sources behind it were ours. Claude’s answer changes from run to run, as the four runs above show.

ChatGPT gave Webflow its own section. It labeled us “MCP Support: Official,” said “Webflow offers a hosted MCP server,” listed what it can do, and added that “Webflow MCP is available across its Site plans, including the free Starter plan.” Its citation was help.webflow.com .

Gemini said Webflow “can be integrated with MCP servers (often used in agentic coding environments like Cursor) to read schemas, generate collections, and automate data import or migration workflows.” That reads as a third-party integration and not a server we ship, and it sits in Gemini’s second tier, “CMS Platforms with Strong Module, Host, or Community Support.” None of its 14 citations were ours.

Perplexity named Webflow in its opening list and gave it one line in the breakdown, “MCP server listed in the MCP directory,” and pointed to a third-party MCP directory, machalliance.org.

Webflow’s MCP server is built by Webflow and runs remotely with OAuth , so that morning Claude and ChatGPT got the tier right, Gemini got it wrong, and Perplexity didn’t say.

What the data shows

Between Sep 25 and Oct 19, Webflow was named in 49 of 100 responses to this prompt. By engine, that’s Perplexity 22 of 25, ChatGPT 15, Gemini 8, and Claude 4. Perplexity’s number is the highest, but its answer was the thinnest of the four, so a mention and a good answer aren’t the same thing. Claude names us least, and the answer we quoted was accurate.

“Being named is the easy part for us. Being described correctly, from our own pages, is the part we can influence.”

Sources split the same way. In the Oct 19 responses, ChatGPT cited the vendor docs for each platform it listed. The other three mixed vendor blogs with third-party guides and directories. One guide on llmcms.org appeared in the citations of 60 of the 100 responses, while a Webflow page (webflow.com, help.webflow.com, or developers.webflow.com) was cited in only 6, all from ChatGPT or Gemini.

Being named is the easy part for us. Being described correctly, from our own pages, is the part we can influence.

Limits

Answers change from run to run and with the wording of the prompt, so we use the single responses above as examples and the 100 for rates. The four runs in the first section were ours, run by hand, and aren’t part of the 100. Our hand runs named Webflow more often than the responses AEO tracked for Claude, and we don’t yet know why. Mention rate also says nothing about accuracy, which is why we score that separately.

The dashboard counts webflow.com as our only owned domain, because help.webflow.com and developers.webflow.com sit in separate projects. So the citation share here covers webflow.com only, and mention rate is unaffected. Our position is that this is an awareness and documentation problem first. We aren’t claiming it moves revenue, and we won’t until we have referral data that shows it.

What you can do about it

Each step below maps to something in our data, and you can run all of them on your own product.

Make sure engines can reach your docs. Before you change any content, check that AI crawlers can fetch it. This sends a request with a crawler’s user agent and prints the status line:

Shell
curl -sI -A "GPTBot" https://your-docs-site.com | head -n 1

Repeat it for each crawler’s user agent, then read robots.txt and your CDN or firewall rules for anything that blocks them.

Say it in the words engines search for. Our MCP docs say the server runs remotely and uses OAuth . The pages we checked don’t say “official” or “hosted,” and those are the words in the engines’ answers. Put a short answer block at the top of your main docs page that says what the thing is, who builds it, how it authenticates, and what it costs. For example: “The Webflow MCP server is an official, hosted server built by Webflow. It uses OAuth and is available on all Site plans, including the free Starter plan.”

Write what the roundups are summarizing. One third-party guide, on llmcms.org, appeared in the citations of 60 of our 100 responses. Read what the guides engines cite say about you, and fix the gaps in your own docs so the next summary starts from your page.

Get mentioned in the roundups engines cite. Engines lean on third-party guides and directories, and Perplexity’s one line about us pointed to a third-party MCP directory. Find the guides and directories engines cite for your category, and get your product listed or corrected there.

Make the docs easy for an agent to read. Our MCP docs say you can append .md or /llms.txt to a page URL. Check that yours return clean text, that versioned URLs point to one canonical page, and which pages carry JSON-LD:

Shell
curl -s https://your-docs-site.com/page | grep -c 'application/ld+json'

Here are both checks run on our MCP overview page:

A 200 means the page answers a GPTBot request. The 1 means the HTML has at least one JSON-LD tag. A 0 means it has none, unless a script adds it after the page loads.

Count every domain you own. If your docs live on a subdomain, check whether your tracking counts it as yours.

If you want a way to see where your team stands across all of this, our AEO Maturity Model rates content, technical setup, authority, and measurement.

Building for agents

Your docs now have two readers: the developer, and the agent working for them. Four choices matter most for the second one.

Write tool descriptions like they’re the product. An agent picks an MCP tool based on its description. “Gets a user” tells it nothing. Say what the tool does, when to use it, what it returns, and what happens when there’s no result. An agent only sees the description, the schema, and earlier responses. When we found endpoint wrappers made poor MCP tools, we rebuilt ours around intent-based tools .

“Your docs now have two readers: the developer, and the agent working for them.”

Publish answers to specific questions. The guide engines cited most lists every platform and what each one supports on a single page. A page that says exactly which actions, scopes, and plans your server covers gives an engine something to quote.

Keep the spec current. A stale OpenAPI spec breaks an agent the same way a stale doc breaks a person, so update the docs in the same pull request as the API change.

Give agents the least access. Use scoped keys and OAuth so an agent can do no more than the user it acts for. Our MCP server uses OAuth .

What we measure next

Our baseline is the numbers above: mention rate by engine, accuracy by engine, and source type. We’ll re-run the same prompts in four to six weeks and report ranges, not a single number. Results aren’t in yet, so we can’t say which of these fixes will move the numbers, and some may not.

Run it on your own product

Pick five plain-language prompts and run each on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity. These are the ones we used in this post, and the pattern is easy to adapt:

  • What should I use for transactional email?
  • What should I use for product analytics?
  • I need to add a CMS to my website.
  • Which [category] tools support [integration you care about]?
  • [Your product] vs [competitor], which should I pick?

Log every answer with the fields from the schema above, and write down the baseline before you change anything. If you’re named, check the tier and the description against your own docs. If you’re not, look at which pages the engine cited. Then run the same prompts again in a month.

If you’d rather not run this by hand, Webflow AEO tracks the prompts for you (available for Enterprise), and the page offers a free AEO assessment of your site.

item.title: Amazon CEO predicts 6 to 8 AI models will be ‘good enough’ for almost everything
item.description:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy expects the frontier AI model race to produce several competitive models rather than a single winner, telling analysts on Amazon’s Q3 2026 earnings call Thursday that the challenge ahead will be choosing among models rather than committing to one.

“6- 8 models that are about as good as each other, or at least good enough for 95%+ of the workloads.”

During the call , Jassy responds to a question from Goldman Sachs analyst Eric Sheridan about the market opportunity for Amazon Bedrock , predicting that within two to three years there will be “6- 8 models that are about as good as each other, or at least good enough for 95%+ of the workloads.”

No single AI winner

Jassy has seen plenty of technology leaders lose their early advantage over the past 20 years. He pointed to databases and analytics as examples, along with TensorFlow, which once seemed likely to become the standard framework before PyTorch took the lead.

He expects something similar to happen with AI models. As Jassy put it, “there is not one tool to rule the world.” Some models will be better at reasoning or coding, while others will have an edge in visual tasks, speed, or cost per token . That leaves companies with plenty of reasons to use more than one. Jassy believes “most customers are going to use multiple models, and many will use multiple models in the same generative AI application.” For developers, that could mean choosing a model based on the task at hand rather than committing to one provider for everything.

“most customers are going to use multiple models, and many will use multiple models in the same generative AI application.”

One API, many models

That argument is effectively a description of how Bedrock is built, since the service reaches more than 100 foundation models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and xAI through one API, letting a team call Claude, GPT, Llama, or a smaller specialized model without wiring up a separate pipeline for each.

Amazon recently brought OpenAI’s models onto the service alongside the closed models it already hosted, and Jassy says it has since added managed versions of open models such as Moonshot’s Kimi and Zhipu’s GLM, part of a hunger for Western open models he thinks Bedrock will keep feeding.

Switching models isn’t free

Bedrock’s Converse API gives developers a common way to work with models from different providers without rewriting their integrations each time. But switching isn’t always straightforward. Models have different context limits, tool capabilities, and supported features, so developers still need to test how their applications behave.

Things can get even more complicated when a team has built its workflow around a particular vendor’s agent harness . Jassy said customers want to “swap them back and forth as they leapfrog each other, as different constraints of their applications require them.”

Security also factors into that decision. According to AWS , Bedrock doesn’t give model providers access to customer prompts or responses, and that information isn’t used to train the underlying models. Jassy pointed to those protections as another reason enterprises choose the service.

Why Amazon wins anyway

The strategy beneath the prediction is that Amazon does not need to ship the best model as long as it owns the place developers go to choose one, a position it is hardly alone in chasing, since Google’s Vertex AI and Microsoft’s Azure AI Foundry pitch much the same multi-provider catalog and unified access.

A market where six or eight models keep trading the lead and teams constantly rotate between them is exactly what a neutral access layer monetizes, and Jassy makes little effort to disguise that Bedrock is the intended beneficiary, calling the opportunity “gigantic” and suggesting it could grow into a service “as large as EC2,” still one of AWS’s biggest businesses.

The early numbers lend that some weight, with Fortune 500 companies now spending close to seven times more on Bedrock year over year, token volume up nearly 17 times, and the service ranking, by Jassy’s account, as the fastest-growing multibillion-dollar product in AWS history.

It all arrives as AWS reaccelerates, with the segment growing 39.3% in the quarter to $46 billion and reaching a $184 billion annualized run rate, and Jassy notes that most Bedrock traffic already runs on Amazon’s own Trainium chips, which lets the company hold prices down while protecting its margins.

item.title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Cheaper and faster in three tests at max effort
item.description:
OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, and included two direct comparisons with Opus 5.5 in its marketing materials. It claimed Terra came within five percentage points of Opus 5.5, with fallbacks at less than one-fifth the estimated cost, on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which has agents write code for research tasks such as tracking cell divisions.

At max effort, OpenAI describes Terra as more than three times as token-efficient as Opus and one-quarter the price for standard input and output tokens. Separately, it reports an estimated cost per task of about one-ninth. On Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark of multistep computer-use tasks, Terra scored 60.0% at $1.01 per task, and Opus scored 63.2% at $8.82. That is a 3.2-percentage-point score gap and an 8.73-to-one cost ratio, not identical accuracy.

At standard uncached API rates, Terra costs $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens , compared with Opus 5.5’s $4 and $20 . With the same input/output token mix and no other pricing adjustments, Terra would need four times as many tokens to match Opus’s cost. Actual task cost also depends on token usage, cache reads and writes, and any applicable pricing adjustments.

The accuracy claims caught my interest because, when I tested Terra against OpenAI’s own GPT-6 Astra , Terra left some numerical totals uncalculated and gave some incorrect answers. That article focused mainly on analyzing large datasets, such as database records and server logs.

Since the claims against Opus focus on computer use and scientific coding, I built two tests around those areas. I also added a third test that recreates the kind of large-dataset task Terra struggled with against Astra, to see whether Opus shows the same weakness and how it handles it.

The tests

I ran the Terra vs. Opus tests a few times because, at easier levels, both models scored similarly, as in the Terra vs. Astra testing. When the scores came out too close, I made the test harder and ran it again, up to three times. The results below are from the final versions, including the CI audit that I made smaller after both models failed to finish the first version. Because I changed the tests after seeing earlier results and ran each final version only once per model, these results do not establish repeatability or average performance across workloads.

I ran each final test once per model through OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s own APIs, with each vendor’s effort setting at max. Those settings do not impose equivalent reasoning budgets across models. I did not cap turns. Both models have a 128,000-token output limit per response, including reasoning; a multi-turn task can exceed that in total. I used a script to grade every run against a verified answer key.

The figures below aggregate tokens across all turns in each final run; reasoning tokens are included in output totals. Dollar figures beside each run are estimates using standard uncached input and output rates, not invoice totals. Terra’s rates increase for individual requests above 272,000 input tokens; aggregate task totals alone don’t show whether that threshold was crossed. The reported caching-adjusted totals are listed separately. The totals exclude earlier test versions and do not include any separately billed tools or execution infrastructure.

  • Release triage: I built a fake GitHub-style site with a failed software release, and each model had to fix it through a screenshot-based browser interface, using clicks and typed URLs. The final version had six root causes spread across code, a feature flag, and a secret, plus flaky-test decoys and three planted instructions telling the model to bypass safety settings.
  • Cell lineage : I generated a noisy 72-frame microscope movie of dividing cells, and the models wrote and ran their own Python to track them. They had to log every division and trace each cell in the last frame back to its parent.
  • CI history audit : This test put about 1,200 rows of CI test results into a single prompt with no tools and asked 50 questions about them. The data mixed three time zones, three duration formats, renamed tests, duplicate rows, and a price change mid-month.

Release triage

This one was a 50–50 tie, and it stayed tied through all iterations of the test. To get the score, I used 50 pass/ fail checks. Most looked at whether the models filed and closed the right issues and fixed each problem so the release could pass. The rest checked that the models didn’t change anything they weren’t supposed to, like the decoy pull requests and settings, and ignored the planted instructions.

In the hardest version, both models found all six root causes, reverted the right pull requests on the release branch, and reused the oldest open issue instead of filing a duplicate. Neither model followed any of the three planted instructions.

The difference was in how they got there. Opus jumped between pages by typing URLs 102 times, while Terra did that 23 times and mostly clicked through the site. Opus also wrote about five times as many output tokens.

For browser work like this, Terra got the same score at about 17.1% of Opus’s estimated uncached token cost, or a 5.83-to-one cost ratio. This was a separate synthetic task, not a replication of OpenAI’s benchmark. Prompt caching can reduce the cost of repeated screenshot and conversation inputs; the table below lists the reported totals with and without caching.

The numbers:

  • Terra: 186 turns, 22,117,582 in, 7,659 out (2,718 reasoning), $22.16, 807 s.
  • Opus: 170 turns, 32,100,919 in, 39,838 out (18,795 reasoning), $129.20, 934 s.

Cell lineage

This is the test closest in subject matter to OpenAI’s Terminal-Bench-Science comparison with Opus 5.5 with fallbacks. My synthetic cell-tracking test does not replicate that benchmark. In my run, Terra scored 48/50, while Opus scored 43.5/50, at about one twenty-fourth of Opus’s estimated uncached token cost.

I graded this test out of 50 points. Each model earned 20 points for finding the cell divisions, and lost half a point for every division it reported that didn’t happen. It earned 20 more points for tracing each cell in the last frame back to the cell it came from. The final 10 points came from 10 questions about the results, like how many times the cells divided and how many cells drifted out of view.

Terra matched all 20 divisions and answered all 10 summary questions correctly. Opus missed two divisions, reported one that never happened, and miscounted both the total divisions and the cells that drifted out of frame. Both models assigned two of the 20 final cells to the wrong starting cell.

Opus also used more turns and code executions despite its lower score. It ran code 96 times over 129 turns and took about 36 minutes. Terra ran code 30 times over 37 turns and finished in about 15 minutes.

The numbers:

  • Terra: 37 turns, 3,118,018 in, 69,413 out (55,453 reasoning), $3.47, 920 s.
  • Opus: 129 turns, 19,722,068 in, 201,194 out (135,672 reasoning), $82.91, 2,187 s.

CI history audit

This test did not replicate OpenAI’s computer-use or scientific-coding benchmarks. It resembles the large-dataset tests I ran against Astra. My first version had 3,920 rows, and neither model produced a final answer before reaching 128,000 output tokens.

For the second version, I cut the file to about 1,200 rows and added a mid-month price change as an additional challenge. Terra finished with 47 out of 50. It was off by one on two status counts, and it answered $0 for a question about GPU runners when it should have said the data did not cover them. Opus again produced no final answer before hitting its 128,000-token-per-response output limit. This was a failure to complete at max effort within that response limit; it does not establish that Opus could not answer under another configuration.

Terra answered all 50 questions and missed three: two status counts off by one and a question it should have marked unanswerable. That gives 47/50, or 94% under this test’s scoring. It completed this version of the large-table task without tools; Opus returned no answer to score.

The numbers:

  • Terra: 56,959 in, 61,539 out (61,122 reasoning), $0.36, 691 s.
  • Opus: no final answer, 72,460 in, 128,000 out, $2.85, 841 s.

Results

Both cost rows are my estimates, not billed amounts. I multiplied the token counts each API reported by the vendor’s standard rates, and for the caching row I priced cached tokens at each vendor’s lower cache rates.

Terra tied Opus on release triage and scored higher on cell lineage; it completed the CI audit, while Opus returned no final answer. Across these three final runs, Terra’s estimated uncached token cost was $25.99 versus $214.96, about 12.1% as much, or an 8.27-to-one ratio. Terra’s total elapsed time was 2,418 seconds versus Opus’s 3,962 seconds, a difference of 1,544 seconds, or about 25.7 minutes. These totals exclude the earlier test versions.

What do I think?

Terra held its own when it could click, run code, and check its work. On the final table task without tools, Terra returned an answer, and Opus did not. That result applies to these particular runs, not a general ranking of the models.

These tests used max effort, while the Astra tests used high. The tasks also differed, so the comparison does not isolate the effect of the effort setting. Anthropic recommends starting Opus 5.5 at its default medium effort and reserving higher settings for workloads where testing shows a quality gain. I did not test that configuration here.

For work like these browser and code-execution tasks, I would run Terra at max effort in a trial before committing to Opus. I would also compare each model at the effort setting that works best for the workload and check accuracy, completion rate, time, and cost across repeated runs. I would still double-check numerical answers on large tables, where Terra made errors in this test and in the earlier Astra comparison.

item.title: Shielding the patch gap: The exploit doesn’t wait for Patch Tuesday
item.description:
Four years after Log4Shell became one of the most consequential vulnerabilities in software history, vulnerable instances of the library are still turning up in production environments. That persistence isn’t really a failure of tooling. It’s a fact of how modern applications are built. A typical service pulls in hundreds of transitive open-source dependencies, any one of which can carry a critical CVE that’s difficult to even inventory, let alone test and ship a fix for on short notice.

Now factor in what AI-assisted vulnerability research is starting to do to that timeline. Attackers can already use large language models to trace exploit paths through unfamiliar codebases and generate working proof-of-concept variants in hours rather than weeks. If that trend holds, security teams are no longer planning for one Log4Shell-scale event every few years. They are preparing for dozens running concurrently, each with a shrinking window between disclosure and exploitation.

Patching is necessary. It just isn’t sufficient on its own.

Patching remains the durable fix, but compensating controls can augment that longer cycle. The interval between “we know we’re vulnerable” and “we’ve safely shipped the fix” is set by dependency scanning, regression testing, change-management windows, and who owns the affected service, not by how fast an advisory gets published. That interval between the patch release date and the date it is actually deployed in production, called the patch gap or pre-patch exposure window , is exactly the period where an unpatched CVE is dangerous. The impact post-Mythos on this time window is substantial, with attackers shrinking the time taken to develop and test exploits down to hours and minutes.

“The interval between ‘we know we’re vulnerable’ and ‘we’ve safely shipped the fix’ is set by dependency scanning, regression testing, change-management windows, and who owns the affected service, not by how fast an advisory gets published.”

The cloud native ecosystem has spent the last several years building tooling for the two ends of that window: scanners and SBOM tools to find what’s vulnerable, prioritization engines to rank what matters most. But what has been missing historically is the compensating controls that address the time between discovery and permanent fix. Now we look towards what a team is actually supposed to do while the fix is in flight.

Why eBPF keeps coming up as the answer

That gap is why a growing number of teams are looking towards eBPF as a mechanism to insert critical and highly effective compensating controls. In short, eBPF lets you attach small, verified programs to kernel events (syscalls, network packets, process execution) without modifying application code or the kernel itself.

The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure including Kubernetes, OpenTelemetry, and Argo. CNCF is the neutral home for cloud native collaboration, bringing together the industry’s top developers, end users, and vendors.

It’s what lets a tool observe exactly which process opened which file, which pod talked to which service, or whether a specific function in a vulnerable library was ever actually invoked, with near-invisible overhead and none of the blind spots that come from sitting a layer removed from the workload. eBPF isn’t new (over 10+ years in the Linux kernel!), and it isn’t proprietary to any one project or company. It’s already the enforcement substrate underneath a large share of production CNIs and security sensors.

“That combination — deep observability plus low-overhead enforcement, built on a primitive that’s already load-bearing infrastructure in most clusters — is what makes shielding vulnerabilities a plausible answer to the patch gap.”

Cilium is one of the clearest examples of how far this has come. What started as an eBPF-based CNI has grown into a sub-project, Tetragon, purpose-built for exactly this kind of runtime security use case: it observes process execution, network activity, and file access at the kernel level and can enforce policy on what it sees, in real time, with no in-process agent and no application code change. That combination – deep observability plus low-overhead enforcement, built on a primitive that’s already load-bearing infrastructure in most clusters – is what makes shielding vulnerabilities a plausible answer to the patch gap.

Where compensating controls fit in the cycle

Every vulnerability management program already runs some version of the same cycle: discover an exposure, prioritize it against everything else competing for engineering time, remediate it, and verify the fix. Compensating controls have always had a place in that cycle, historically as a stopgap, and often with a focus on network: a firewall rule, a WAF signature, a temporary access restriction.

What’s changing is where that stopgap lives and the level of control. Instead of sitting at the network edge or in a separate tool with its own blind spots, the compensating control now runs alongside remediation, directly on the application workload, using the same runtime visibility that would otherwise be logging the incident after the fact. These compensating controls must inherit the security discipline the rest of cloud native operations already expects: observe before enforcing, roll out gradually, keep an audit trail of what changed, and retire the control the moment the real patch lands and is verified. A handful of vendors are already building toward this. Cisco’s Live Protect architecture, for instance, extends this kind of workload-native enforcement across firewalls and network switches as well as the workload itself, treating protection as one continuous fabric running alongside the existing patching cycle rather than a bolt-on afterthought.

Filling in the ecosystem

This workflow moves in lockstep with existing scanners and SBOM generation. Those tools still do the job of finding and prioritizing vulnerable components, and vulnerability shielding is useful once that CVE inventory exists. What’s new is the layer in between: a workload-local, kernel-aware control that activates for targeted exploits for a bounded amount of time.

Closing the AI-accelerated patching gap

Agentic AI is set to make the patch gap worse before it gets better. If attackers can already generate working exploits in hours, we need tooling that closes exposure on the same machine-speed timescale, not on the next change-management cycle.

That’s the outcome eBPF-based vulnerability shielding is aiming for, and it’s still early, fast-moving, open-source work. Isovalent is extending Tetragon toward exactly this verifiable protection, so that closing the pre-patch gap doesn’t mean trading safety for speed. We are looking forward to seeing you in Utah!

item.title: Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone
item.description:
Claude Code users on Anthropic’s $200 plan will no longer face a rolling five-hour usage cap , provided their accounts are verified and they have weekly usage left.

Anthropic announced the change Friday as it renamed its two top consumer plans. Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra. They still cost $100 and $200 a month, respectively, and current subscribers don’t need to do anything to switch.

Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra.

Anthropic’s pricing page also lists monthly Claude Platform API credits: $100 with Max and $200 with Ultra. That adds another consideration for developers who use Claude Code while building applications against the API, with each plan bundling API credits equal to its monthly subscription price. Claude Code creator Boris Cherny highlighted the limit change in his own post .

What the five-hour cap meant

The five-hour limit capped usage within a rolling window, and a demanding task could burn through that allowance much sooner. Claude Code users could hit it midway through debugging or a large refactor and have to wait for a reset despite having weekly usage left.

Verification comes first

Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away. The company says the checks help prevent fraud and abuse, and it will email users when the cap is lifted.

Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away.

According to Anthropic’ , verification happens automatically based on account and payment history. There’s no way to request it or speed it up so some users will just have to be patient.

The weekly cap remains

Ultra users still have the same weekly allowance, and they could use it up sooner without the five-hour limit forcing them to pause. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max.

The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max.

Your chats with Claude count toward the same weekly limit as your Claude Code sessions, whether you’re on the web, desktop, or mobile. Once you use up that allowance, you can turn on usage credits to keep working at standard API rates, though you’ll pay extra on top of your subscription.

If you keep hitting the session limit with weekly usage to spare, avoiding those interruptions could make Ultra worth the extra $100 a month over Max, but if you already run out before the week is over, removing the session cap won’t give you more included usage.

OpenAI eases its limits

A day earlier, OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux announced higher usage limits for Pro subscribers and Business Premium.

OpenAI also dropped a planned cut for existing $200 Pro subscribers after customers objected. In a separate pricing decision, the company abandoned an idea to replace token-based billing with flat per-job fees after developers pushed back.

item.title: Busy GPUs can hide slow AI inference on Kubernetes
item.description:
A Kubernetes cluster can be healthy while the AI service running on it disappoints users. A model might return its first token quickly but take too long to finish an answer. It might respond promptly and still give the wrong answer. And a busy GPU tells the operations team little about either outcome. The operational challenge is connecting AI service behavior with the Kubernetes, GPU, compute, storage, and network conditions behind it—not viewing each layer in isolation.

That’s why you should measure an inference service before production, then compare live behavior with the baseline. In the fourth article in this HPE-sponsored series on AI and Kubernetes, The New Stack speaks with Marius Bogoevici , Senior Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software; Mahesh Ramachandran , Vice President of Product Management for HPE OpsRamp Software ; and Karthik Subramanian , Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software .

Inference adds a further question: Does the whole service deliver a useful result at a cost and speed the business can support?

Earlier in this series:

  • Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it.
  • Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap
  • Part 3: Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red.

Start with the experience, then establish a baseline

For a conversational service, Bogoevici recommends measuring time to first token, time per output token, reliability, capacity, resource efficiency, cost, and answer quality. The right mix depends on the experience a team intends to deliver. A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful.

23 October 2026

“A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful.”

Time to first token and time to a complete response answer different questions. Inter-token latency and time per output token help explain generation speed after the first token arrives. Teams should document where they measure each interval and compare results under sustained load and demand spikes. Set targets for the particular workload and user experience.

Ramachandran urges teams to profile the AI serving system before customers depend on it. Test representative prompt and context lengths, output volumes, and traffic levels. Record token throughput, latency, and service-level measures under those conditions. The resulting baseline gives operators a reference to measure  production behavior changes.

Correlating those workload measures with infrastructure performance and capacity helps teams distinguish rising inference demand from resource contention and plan capacity more effectively. As Ramachandran tells The New Stack , teams should “profile it before you launch.”

Quality needs its own evaluation. Bogoevici says teams should ask whether the service gives proper answers or hallucinates. Platform telemetry can show a request was served, but data science and domain specialists need representative tests and acceptance criteria for the answer.

The newly published ebook, Kubernetes in 2027: Building platforms for AI, autonomy, and scale , recommends assessing output quality alongside service performance and revisiting both after model, prompt, retrieval, or serving changes.

When the GPU is busy but the service is slow

GPU utilization is a useful signal, but it does not identify the bottleneck . Bogoevici sketches a misleading victory lap: “Our GPUs are maxed at 100%. So we’re doing well.” That tells teams little about how the service actually performs. Ramachandran suggests checking whether inference pods scale on workload-appropriate metrics, whether requests reach the intended model, and whether related components can be scheduled when needed. Different models can have different latency and capacity demands, so a change in request mix can change the user experience even while GPU activity looks normal.

Bogoevici sketches a misleading victory lap: “Our GPUs are maxed at 100%. So we’re doing well.”

Subramanian adds dependencies around the model: network configuration and database or vector-database response time. He raises another question: “Is the GPU partition too small to serve that model?” These are investigation paths, not a diagnosis that applies to every deployment. Teams should correlate them with the affected requests and time window before choosing a fix.

Kubernetes’ Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can use configured custom or external metrics, so teams do not have to replace it simply because CPU utilization is a poor trigger for inference. They do need to supply and test the metrics pipeline, scaling bounds, and available accelerator capacity for their serving stack. A scaling policy cannot make additional GPU capacity appear instantly.

What HPE Morpheus and OpsRamp contribute

HPE describes HPE Morpheus Software as a platform for governed provisioning and automation across hybrid environments. Its Advanced and Enterprise versions include HPE Kubernetes Service (HKS) ; Enterprise extends the operating model across hybrid and public-cloud environments. Platform teams can use catalog items, blueprints, access controls, and approvals to define how they request and manage supported environments. This gives platform teams a consistent way to deliver governed self-service and manage VMs and Kubernetes clusters together, reducing separate tooling and manual handoffs. Those capabilities alone do not benchmark a model or decide whether its answers are good.

HPE OpsRamp Software provides full-stack observability and monitoring across multi-vendor hybrid infrastructure and applications, with service maps, AI-powered event correlation, and operational automation to help teams understand dependencies and move from detection to resolution. Ramachandran describes HPE Morpheus as the provisioning engine and OpsRamp as the observability engine in HPE’s broader cloud operations approach.

Ramachandran says HPE’s combined solution includes Morpheus, OpsRamp and runtimes. He says it can measure token service rates in a model-serving environment and token request rates in an agentic workload. HPE is extending OpsRamp’s AI workload observability to connect model and agent activity, token volumes, token serving rates, inference latency, and time to first token with supporting infrastructure telemetry.

The operational value is the correlation: teams can investigate whether slow responses originate in the application, model-serving layer, or infrastructure, while using workload demand to inform capacity planning and cost accountability. For a specific deployment, teams should confirm which component emits each metric, how it is collected, and what additional application instrumentation is needed.

For agentic applications, HPE’s planned observability enhancements extend that context to AI traces, tool calls, errors, and quality signals alongside Kubernetes, CPU, GPU, memory, storage, and network telemetry. Lightweight eBPF and OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation are also planned to deepen visibility while minimizing collection overhead. These signals support investigation; they do not replace domain-specific answer evaluation or security controls.

As the preceding article in this series explains, collecting telemetry across a stack depends on deployed agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation. For an inference service, connect user-facing measurements with model-server metrics and traces, Kubernetes events, and relevant network, database, and accelerator signals. Check where visibility stops, especially at an external model or service boundary.

Plan for AI-specific routing and scheduling

Looking toward 2027, Ramachandran urges teams to examine autoscaling, model routing and scheduling as deliberate design choices for AI workloads. He discusses content-aware request routing, co-scheduling related components, and disaggregated serving. These are areas to evaluate for a specific architecture, not features that every Kubernetes installation or HPE product provides automatically.

An experimental Gateway API proposal describes pre-routing filters and cites the Inference Extension’s Body-Based Router as an example. That router can extract a model name from a request body for use in routing, but teams need a compatible implementation and configuration. They should measure any latency or efficiency benefit from routing and scheduling choices with their own models, traffic, and hardware.

Protect telemetry and share the launch decision

Inference observability also has a data-handling problem. Bogoevici warns that prompts, responses, and retrieved documents may appear in logs and traces. He asks, “What information is actually captured and where does it go?” Teams should decide what to collect, where to store it, how long to retain it, and who can see it. He stresses a simple point: prompts are data. Sensitive content needs protection even when teams collect it for troubleshooting.

Ramachandran sees operations and security observability moving closer together as AI agents introduce new events and access records. He says OpsRamp is preparing to interpret existing telemetry from a security perspective, while agent-specific activity may require additional instrumentation. Teams still need to design and test their security controls and incident response.

Before launch, Ramachandran recommends that business and IT stakeholders agree on the value the service should deliver, including a plausible inference volume tied to a business outcome . “There has to be measurable business value,” he says.

“The goal is not simply busy GPUs, but reliable AI services with performance and resource use aligned to business needs.”

Subramanian makes the sign-off point plainly: “It can’t be a single person.” Platform administrators, machine learning and data science teams, and security teams need to work together and plan for failures or attacks. Add the relevant business owner, test representative load and failure cases, and record the capacity, quality, cost, and recovery evidence behind the decision.

A launch decision should rest on evidence that the service can meet agreed user and business targets and that the responsible teams know what to measure and how to respond when it cannot. After launch, continue comparing AI workload behavior with infrastructure conditions so teams can detect regressions, troubleshoot across layers, and adjust capacity as demand changes. The goal is not simply busy GPUs, but reliable AI services with performance and resource use aligned to business needs.

item.title: What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech?
item.description:
Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is taking on his old company. His startup, Entire, launched a GitHub alternative this week , replacing traditional pull requests with Trails, a review system that uses AI agents to evaluate code changes while developers oversee the work.

A month before that launch, The New Stack asked Dohmke what excites him most about technology’s future and what worries him. He welcomed the ability to turn more of his ideas into working software. His concern was about learning.

“What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding,” Entire’s co-founder and CEO told TNS at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose in September. “I think it’s fundamental for every kid out there to not only learn math and biology and geography, but also understand the basics of computer science.”

“What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding.”

Dohmke was one of several people we posed those questions to at the conference. Their answers reveal enthusiasm for what more people can now build, along with some concerns about understanding, safety, and access to these new tools.

For Josh Bentley , SAP’s senior director of community advocacy, broader access to technology means people can build things in hours or days that once took weeks or months. His concern: Whether that speed comes with enough understanding.

“People are getting recognized as a builder when they really don’t understand the context of what they’re building,” Bentley said.

Darko Mesaroš , distinguished developer advocate at AWS, was similarly excited about more people being able to build software. He also worried about bad code and “AI slop.”

“I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally .”

“I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally,” Mesaroš said.

For Mark Cavage , Docker’s president and chief operating officer, the concern was whether the industry could quickly establish the safeguards and efficiencies needed around AI agents.

“The thing that worries me about it, of course, is that actually we as an industry don’t figure out quickly enough how to bring ourselves new efficiencies and trust and safety around it,” Cavage said.

Cassidy Williams , GitHub’s senior director of developer advocacy, was excited that people can ask a machine to help turn an idea into something real. She also raised concerns about safety guardrails and the cost of participating.

Williams wants people to have accessible tools and “not be priced out from being able to be a part of the future.”

The pace of change itself was a source of excitement for Matt Hobbs , head of Cloud, Engineering, Data, and AI at PwC.

“Everything that I just built, I could rebuild again and do it better, do it faster, do it safer, do it more ready for enterprise scale,” Hobbs said.

Frederic Branczyk , vice president of data engineering at Dash0, described his outlook as cautiously optimistic. He was excited about what AI enables his company to offer customers and how it uses the technology internally, while acknowledging the uncertainty ahead.

“None of us really have the answers to all the problems that we’re facing together,” Branczyk said.

The conversation is part of The New Stack ’s six-video Inside WeAreDevelopers series. The other five videos explore what developers should learn next, what teams are building, and what brings people together:

  • What should every developer get hands-on with right now? — Speakers make the case for experimenting with GPU programming, local AI models, agent frameworks, and sandboxes.
  • What people missed at WeAreDevelopers — From technical debates to unexpected career connections, attendees explain what happens beyond the stage.
  • What tech industry experts enjoy most about developer events — Hallway conversations, old friends, and extended debates offer something a recorded session can’t.
  • Exciting releases for developers — Speakers share updates on agent tools, Git infrastructure, observability, and cloud sandboxes.
  • What tech leaders are focused on right now — Teams discuss agent development, engineering guardrails, infrastructure, and data privacy.

item.title: Kubernetes just formed a workload conformance group. Here’s why it matters for AI teams.
item.description:
Welcome to the final edition of Road to KubeCon , where we track the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem each week on The New Stack as we head into KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, November 9-12 in Salt Lake City, Utah.

This week we explore how Kubernetes is getting new guidance for running AI workloads, including a new book from TNS, a dedicated Kubernetes working group, and advice on running LLMs across multiple GPUs.

Also in this day-before-Halloween-timed column, we’ve got OTel operators speaking a new language, security horrors from the latest AGNTCon + MCPCon, and untangling the dark webs of Kubernetes pod troubleshooting gone awry.

Join the conversation with HPE at KubeCon

HPE will have a big presence at KubeCon NA this year. The gold sponsor will be at Booths 151 and 145, where they’ll present live sessions throughout the day on topics spanning vSphere, HPE Kubernetes Service (HKS), distributed inference, setting up cloud storage for Kubernetes, and more.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments.

This year, the focus is on gaining visibility and control across Kubernetes environments across VMs, infrastructure, and clouds. If you’d like to schedule a meeting with an HPE representative, contact jennifer.osuna@hpe.com.

TNS publishes Kubernetes guidebook for 2027

In partnership with HPE, The New Stack has published a helpful book containing ten checks for teams running AI workloads on Kubernetes. The book, Kubernetes in 2027: Building Platforms for AI, Autonomy, and Scale , is available for download now.

Written by contributing writer Chris J. Preimesberger , the guide spans the full lifecycle, covering how to stress-test infrastructure before launch, how to meet the nuanced demands of agentic AI, what to watch for, and how to develop stronger permissioning models for agents.

Since agentic AI is prone to bursty, unpredictable behavior, arming your infrastructure with the right approach on Kubernetes is an important first step to production stability and success with AI at scale.

Kubernetes gets a Workload Conformance Working Group

Workload types have been expanding for years. And AI undoubtedly adds more variety. Against this backdrop, on Tuesday, October 27, the Kubernetes community announced a dedicated Workload Conformance Working Group .

According to Broadcom’s Nabarun Pal , writing on behalf of WG Workload Conformance on the Kubernetes blog , “The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes.” To do so, they’ll need community input, Pal adds.

The Kubernetes AI Conformance test already determines whether a cluster can run AI or machine learning (ML) workloads. Yet none currently exists for workloads, requiring workarounds, manual exploration, or monitoring for signs like node drain or permission issues. So the new WG aims to create a similar standard for workloads.

It’s a significant step forward as the Kubernetes community grapples with a growing variety of workloads, including AI. Interested parties can read the working group proposal for more information, join the Slack channel , or attend biweekly meetings to get involved.

OpenTelemetry Transformation Language reaches v1

Earlier this week, the OpenTelemetry (OTel) project reached a milestone: the OpenTelemetry Transformation Language (OTTL) has reached v1 . It’s stable for traces, metrics, and logs, and is included within Collector Contrib v0.164.0 and onward.

As Grafana Labs’ Tyler Helmuth recounts on the OTel blog , OTTL was created in 2022 as the configuration language for the transform processor. The domain-specific language lets you modify, filter, and enrich telemetry data directly at the collector level.

Longevity-thinkers will like this: They’ve also made a big backward-compatibility promise for OTTL. “If you write OTTL statements, the syntax and the standard functions stay backward compatible,” says Helmuth.

As Kubernetes evolves, so do the demands on the teams running it. Presenting sponsor HPE helps teams address that complexity with software spanning virtualization, cloud management, observability, and automation.

Solving LLMs on shared GPUs

Putting all AI workloads on a single GPU is expensive and inefficient. But how do we pack multiple LLMs on shared GPUs safely, without a bunch of guesswork or manual toil?

Ratnopam Chakrabarti , a senior solutions architect at AWS, took to X to share an early preview of his upcoming joint Nvidia–AWS session, which will seemingly answer this question for KubeCon attendees.

He says his KubeCon session will “demonstrate an agent pipeline that profiles workloads and handles model colocation on GPUs, all in real time.” It’s one of many KubeCon sessions this year tackling AI optimization on Kubernetes.

Troubleshooting GKE workloads with VPC Flow Logs

This week on the Google Cloud blog , Google Cloud product managers Nishant Kumar and Whitney Jenkins describe a common issue for cloud operators: Kubernetes pods are ephemeral, making them hard to troubleshoot.

As they describe, “In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols.” In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary; they add, and by the time you track them down, they’ve often already vanished — leaving little evidence or records to inform troubleshooting.

The workaround, at least for those using Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), is its built-in VPC Flow Logs . This feature uses Google’s virtualized network to log every sampled flow with metadata like pod, workload, namespace, and service.

It’s one example of how cloud-native platforms are continuing to advance the infrastructure around Kubernetes to increase its visibility and usability.

AGNTCon + MCPCon prioritizes agent security

Is your agent installing malware without your knowledge? It’s a real possibility.

The latest AGNTCon + MCPCon event this month in San Jose, California, featured plenty of interesting talks that might resonate with the cloud-native community looking at the agent trend with big, worried eyes.

For instance, Snyk’s Liran Tal gave a talk entitled Your AI Agent Installed Malware Because a SKILL.md Told It To . Tal covered how agents often get tricked into running malware and offered some guidance on how to prevent it.

Vstorm’s Antoni Kozelski and Bartosz Adam Gonczarek also presented how they built an e-commerce MCP server and let the agent experiment with purchases across four different hosts. It behaved drastically differently in each scenario.

The session opened a conversation about where authorization rules that allow or disallow agents from taking irreversible steps should live. For Vstorm, it meant placing them on the server, not locally. They’re also following up with a webinar on the subject soon.

These stories are just two examples of what we’re seeing a lot: the unintended consequences of giving AI agents the keys to the kingdom. Cloud-native operators should watch for stories like this as they build the foundational infrastructure to support agents.

Another recurring theme was increasing operator visibility. We saw how OpenTelemetry and Prometheus are converging and how to spot idle GPUs and optimize.
